clues: Irish physicians Robert Adams (1827) and William Stokes (1846) detailed recurrent episodes of sudden fainting or seizure-like movements and this condition. This is still known as Adams-Stokes Syndrome.
In 1873, Alfred Lewis Galabin reported what is recognized as the first human documentation of this using an apexcardiogram in a 34 year old patient with near-fainting spells

Initially, Wenckebach worked at a zoological institute with an interest in pathology, but due to his color blindness redirected his interests to physiology. He started as a rural physician in the Netherlands and spent hours listening to heart rhythms and tracking pulses in his patients. He helped define one type of this condition.

In 1735, physician Gaspar Casal first described the illness among poor peasants in Asturias and called it mal de la rosa. He noted distinctive dark, scaly skin lesions around the neck, later known as Casal's necklace

Public health researcher, Dr Goldberger observed that adding milk, eggs, and fresh foods to orphanages and asylums prevented and cured the illness. In a prison study, restricting inmates to a corn-heavy, low-protein diet induced this disease in several volunteers. To prove this disease wasn't contagious, Goldberger and his colleagues held what became famous as 'filth parties,' ingesting or exposing themselves to secretions and waste from patients without contracting the disease
This nutritional deficiency is known by the triad of dementia, dermatitis, and diarrhea. The necessary nutrient is used to build NAD and NADP.

Historically, this was known as 'spotted fever'. In 1904, this disease struck New York City and between March and May, 436 deaths were reported. Children were especially vulnerable and survivors often faced lifelong disabilities such as blindness, deafness, or partial paralysis

Oscar Wilde had a longstanding ear problem that worsened during his 1895–1897 imprisonment. In October 1900, he underwent a radical middle-ear surgery in his Paris hotel room and it is suspected that he developed this disease leading to his death in November 1900.

Before Heinrich Quincke introduced the lumbar puncture in 1891, doctors relied on physical maneuvers to diagnose this disease. Around this time, Russian physician Vladimir Kernig and Polish pediatrician Josef Brudzinski both published descriptions of involuntary leg-flexing reflexes in affected patients.

Between 2005 and 2009, the World Anti-Doping Agency placed this medication on its prohibited list. While it does not enhance athletic performance, it alters steroid metabolism in urine and could mask the use of banned anabolic steroids. It was later removed from the banned list due to advances in lab testing.

In the 1970s, a Cornell endocrinologist traveled to the isolated village of Las Salinas in the Dominican Republic. She studied a group of children known locally as guevedoces who appeared female at birth but developed male anatomy during puberty. Researchers discovered these individuals lacked a key enzyme. Hearing about this study, the head researcher at Merck decided to develop a drug that mimicked this genetic trait
This medication was first approved in 1992 for treating benign prostatic hyperplasia. Five years later, it was approved for male pattern hair loss.

This syndrome became famous during the Vietnam War and was known as 'Da Nang lung' because so many affected casualties pass through medical facilities there. Early cases had devastating survival rates with as many as 8 in 10 patients dying.

In the mid-1960s, a young surgical resident named David Ashbaugh and pulmonologist Thomas Petty noticed 12 patients whose developed this syndrome after unrelated triggers. They wrote a paper unifying these cases but major American medical journals dismissed their findings and rejected the manuscript. They sent the paper to the British journal The Lancey who published it in 1967. This became one of the most cited papers in critical care history.
Early on, standard practice was to set ventilators to push 12-15ml/kg of air into the lungs. In 2000, a landmark study proved that using 6ml/kg dramatically cut death rates.
